articleTitle: The generic reusable component: an approach to reuse hierarchical OO designs
abstract: The authors have developed a framework for the specification of generic reusable components existing wholly at the architectural design level. All features of the component necessary for its effective use are stored with the component, including documentation, design rationale, formal specifications, reuse history and access rights. Design-level genericity is introduced to widen the scope of applicability of the component. At design level a generic component is a partially defined object whose behavior depends on the behavior of parts that are not yet designed. It is shown how to integrate the design of such components into the full HOOD life-cycle method.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Uniformity and invariance in support of re-use
abstract: Noting that software reuse depends on the availability of engineering concepts for its support, the author introduces some of those engineering concepts and two derived notions: uniformity and invariance. He argues that both of these notions play an important role in the industrialization of the underlying engineering concepts.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: SRSGEN-a software reuse tool for large scale applications
abstract: Noting that success in reuse is limited by a need for new tools to help capture and retrieve various life cycle products, the author discusses how SRSGEN (software reuse system generator) accomplishes this goal. Expected benefits of the SRSGEN approach include more flexibility in responding to customer needs, faster response time in developing new system features, and better streamlining of the overall development process by reducing proliferation of unnecessary variation of general-purpose software modules. Throughout the paper, a switching system is taken as one of the examples of a large-scale software application.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Regression analysis of reusable program components
abstract: An integrated regression analysis is proposed for the reverification of software components that are modified for a new application. The basis for the method is clustering, i.e., automatic identification of the modifications. The clustering is used to formulate a regression fault hypothesis about the existence of a fault in the new component and testing the hypothesis using static and dynamic (execution-based) analysis.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A positive experience with software reuse supported by a software bus framework
abstract: BART, a software bus, was designed to provide flexibility in the development of software systems by promoting component independence. This framework allows components to be constructed independently of the context in which they are to be used, thereby allowing them to be reused in many different situations. The authors' experience in using BART to prototype a system that supports group collaboration between people residing in geographically different places demonstrated the feasibility of this approach. They were able to connect a number of existing components with little effort in a surprisingly short time. They discuss the role BART played in supporting the integration of software components and in enabling them to rapidly prototype a shared space collaboration system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The reuse capability model: a basis for improving an organization's reuse capability
abstract: The author discusses a reuse capability model that is being developed by the Software Productivity Consortium to serve as a basis for understanding and improving an organization's reuse capability. Companies apply the reuse capability model in conjunction with the consortium's reuse adoption process and reuse economics model to aid the organization in making an intelligent business decision on how to practice reuse. The reuse capability model includes an assessment model for identifying an organization's strengths and improvement opportunities and an implementation model to serve as a framework for establishing goals and selecting strategies for evolving an organization's reuse practice. An initial model is described along with the rationale and steps taken in developing it.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: LILEANNA: a parameterized programming language
abstract: LILEANNA, a language for formally specifying and generating Ada packages, extends Ada by introducing two entities, theories and views, and enhancing a third, package specifications. A LILEANNA package, with semantics specified either formally or informally, represents a template for actual Ada package specifications. It is used as the common parent for families of implementations and for version control. A theory is a higher-level abstraction, a concept (or a context), that describes a module's syntactical and semantic interface. A view is a mapping between types, operations, and exceptions. The author describes key elements of the language and presents examples illustrating its applicability in support of a megaprogramming software development paradigm.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A reuse metrics and return on investment model
abstract: It is argued that establishing a realistic return on investment on a reuse program is essential to inserting reuse into a corporate software development process, and that clearly stating the potential benefits of reuse in financial terms has proven to be a powerful motivator. A reuse metrics and return on investment (ROI) model that distinguish the savings and benefits from those already gained through accepted software engineering techniques are defined. Three reuse metrics are derived from readily available and observable software data elements. The metrics are used in the return on investment model to establish sound business justification for reuse.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: On the retrieval of reusable software components
abstract: Starting from the principle of software reusability through formal specifications, the authors suggest a model for the retrieval of reusable components utilizing the search techniques in database management systems. The formal specification language of software components is ASL. Component specifications will be translated into a specification written in the knowledge representation Telos for storage and other manipulation. The retrieval of software components is based on signature matching between the signatures of goal specifications and those of reusable components. In this way, the authors overcome some of the main problems with respect to retrieval such as representation of reusable components, representation of goal specification, and name differences in the software. The retrieval mechanism is supported by the database management system ConceptBase.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design as evolution and reuse
abstract: A process for constructing an information workspace with low-cost access to reusable analysis and design knowledge has been developed and validated. The intent is to support the design and evolution of product families. The process involves three related efforts: techniques to consolidate critical analysis and design information-domain analysis; organization of the information in structured form-technology books; and methods and tools to reuse information. It is concluded that a process for consolidating and reusing design knowledge is powerful by itself, and in the authors' engineering domains, the reuse of analyses and designs is more useful than the reuse of software.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A constructive approach to reuse of conceptual components
abstract: A methodological approach to the design-for-reuse process is presented. Reusability at the conceptual design level is considered, and tools for preparing reusable components to be exploited for designing applications not from scratch, but tailoring and adapting existing components are presented. Reusable components are defined as generic components with associated metacomponents providing guidelines for reuse in a given application.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: People-oriented software reuse: the very thought
abstract: The authors argue for integrating the role of software engineers into existing reuse paradigms and providing tool support to assist problem description and component understanding, selection and adaptation. Empirical studies indicate that these reuse tasks are difficult, even for experienced software engineers. Therefore, guidelines and a high-level architecture for design of tool support based on reports of behavior and problems arising during reuse are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experiences from application of a faceted classification scheme
abstract: Various aspects of the classification and retrieval mechanisms which have been applied in the ESPRIT-2 project REBOOT are discussed. This classification scheme is now being slightly modified due to requirements identified through practical application. The authors first discuss different ways of classification and retrieval in general. Then the classification scheme originally proposed by REBOOT is examined. The authors share their experiences throughout the development and application of this scheme. A proposal for a refined version of the scheme that alleviates some of the shortcomings of the original scheme is presented. Some conclusions are drawn, from their work, and problems which are of primary concern are pointed out.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The REBOOT environment (software reuse)
abstract: The REBOOT Project (reuse based on object oriented techniques) has developed two software development process models (development for reuse and development with reuse) that incorporate reuse specific activities in all phases of the development life-cycle, and a set of tools, the REBOOT environment, to help an organization manage a database of reusable components in support of these two models. The authors discuss the facilities offered by the REBOOT tools, the tool architecture that has been designed to facilitate the tool porting to various database systems, and the tool integration into complete software development environments.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Retrieval of reusable components in a development information system
abstract: A query facility for accomplishing reusable class retrieval from a software information base based on similarity queries is described. Classes are described by the operators and similarity relationships that the query facility uses in its search. In the software information base, both reusable components and their associated development information are described in a knowledge-based formalism. The prototype query system implemented on the software base is described. It uses dynamic relationships about the conceptual closeness of available components to retrieve components that best match the requirements of the application under development.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Object oriented module interconnection languages
abstract: The authors discuss two approaches to a module interconnection language (MIL) for object components. They first look at a prototypical programming language which makes the connectivity between objects explicit by making the specification of the object type identify not just the methods it provides but also those it requires. They then propose an algebra of objects which enables new objects (components) to be built from old and, because the algebra is closed, the new components themselves can be used to build further components.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Polymorphic components for monomorphic languages
abstract: Most procedural programming languages, due to their restricted type systems, do not allow for polymorphic software components in the style of functional languages, although polymorphism greatly increases the potential for component reuse, while guaranteeing the security of strong typing. It is shown how to obtain polymorphic software components for ordinary languages like C or Modula-2. The method is based on generic type inference in a software component library. The source of polymorphism is the use of free (undeclared) names in a component. The analysis algorithm will infer signature schemes, which are analogous to type schemes in functional languages. Signature schemes can be used to check library consistency and make it possible to retrieve components by usage patterns.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experiences from software reuse in industrial process control applications
abstract: The author summarizes the experiences of software reuse gained in a software factory producing application software for industrial control systems. The software reuse has been a prime issue in this factory since the beginning of the 1970s. Knowledge, concepts, product descriptions, product transformations, software processes, and project organizations were typical objects for reuse. Specification algebra (category) and specification-morphism (functor) are thought to bring new issues to the future software reuse. It is argued that how to reuse categories, how to reuse functors between categories, and how to reuse process programming will become central issues in the coming generation of software factories.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Reuse-in-the-large: modeling, specification and management
abstract: The author discusses how reuse-in-the-large happens by reusing a large-scale component (LSC) which contains both large-gain components and large-scale information. The former refers to the source code components such as subsystems or even complete systems; the later refers to the information about the creation of the components. It is claimed that reuse-in-the-large is capable of improving the process of software development and maintenance.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Performance considerations in object-oriented reuse
abstract: The importance of performance considerations in object-oriented reuse is pointed out. It is emphasized that the performance of software systems built through reuse should be predictable from their reconfiguration specifications prior to physical realization. A three-level approach is presented, based on separate models of organizational usage patterns, software component performance characterizations, and hardware performance models. The basic analysis methods are described. The process of establishing static component performance characterizations through measurement is discussed, and a realization of the approach in connection with the REBOOT project is outlined. Conclusions and directions for further work are offered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Enhanced reuse with group decision support systems
abstract: The application of group decision support systems (GDSSs) to domain analysis is proposed so that domain analysis may become a more effective team activity. In a large complex software project, the problems of scale due to the interaction of individuals as team members and the interaction of teams with teams tend to limit the overall effectiveness of an organization. A systematic approach to facilitating these interactions is described. The GDSS methodology used is based on interpretive structural modeling, developed by J.N. Warfield in his 1976 book.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
